identification.summary: Group-IB designates GHOST STADIUM as a Chinese-speaking, financially motivated threat actor running a large phishing and ticket-fraud operation against FIFA World Cup 2026 fans, using a custom React-based kit that clones fifa.com and its single sign-on login flow [S1][S3][S7]. More than 300 of the 4,300+ FIFA-impersonating domains Group-IB tracked are actively running fraudulent infrastructure, with roughly 3,800 more parked or dormant [S3][S4]. Group-IB describes GHOST STADIUM as one of four independent threat actors it identified targeting the tournament, with six fraud schemes in parallel [S1][S4]. This is a fraud/cybercrime cluster, not a state-sponsored APT, per the cited reporting [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Not confirmed; the wider FIFA-impersonating domain registrations date from August 2025 [S1][S3]
identification.notes: Group-IB tracks four independent actors in the World Cup fraud ecosystem; only GHOST STADIUM is named in the cited material, and facts about the other three or about generic 'World Cup scam' reporting by other vendors must not be merged into this cluster [S1][S4]. Silent Push reports a separate hunt for 227 matching phishing domains; its relationship to Group-IB's cluster is not established in the material reviewed [S6]. The 2,513 credential-pair figure appears in secondary reporting; Dataproof attributes the credentials mostly to infostealers (Vidar and Lumma named per that outlet), not to this kit's phishing [S3].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified; assessed by Group-IB as a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking criminal actor [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Group-IB characterizes the actor as Chinese-speaking and financially motivated; the confidence level is not stated in the secondary sources reviewed [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Group-IB-based reporting points to Chinese-language notes in the source code and an interface switching across 11 languages as indirect evidence of a Chinese-speaking developer [S2]. Shared Meta Pixel IDs across 300+ domains link the cluster [S7]. The original Group-IB text could not be opened, so the full basis is unverified.

objectives: Financial gain through fake premium ticket sales, resale of tickets tied to hijacked FIFA accounts, and credential theft; Group-IB estimates premium ticket fraud alone at $71 million to $474 million, with total losses potentially reaching billions [S1][S2][S4]. GovInfoSecurity/BankInfoSecurity report a different range of $470 million to $1 billion [S5].

sectors: Consumers / sports fans (World Cup ticket buyers)
regions: Global (FIFA World Cup 2026 audience; kit supports 11 languages)
targeting.notes: Victims are individual fans buying tickets; FIFA is impersonated rather than breached [S1][S4]. The kit supports 11 languages [S4]. Lures offered tickets as cheap as $60 for seats officially priced in the thousands [S3][S4].

capabilities.summary: Custom React single-page phishing kit closely cloning fifa.com and its single sign-on flow, with an interface supporting 11 languages [S1][S4][S7]. Pages include a parameter (p1:reset:userPassword) that authorizes password reset, letting the attacker lock out the legitimate user after capturing credentials and resell tickets tied to the account [S3]. Traffic is acquired mainly through paid Facebook ads, with Meta Pixel IDs shared across the cluster; Telegram and WhatsApp links are secondary channels [S3][S4][S7]. Infrastructure is large-scale domain registration with hyphenated FIFA-name variants, many parked for later activation [S1][S3]. Related parallel schemes in the wider ecosystem include credential phishing, fake ticket sales and counterfeit merchandise [S1][S4].

diamond.adversary: Chinese-speaking, financially motivated fraud operator; one of four independent actors Group-IB tracks for the tournament [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Custom React phishing kit cloning fifa.com and its SSO flow; password-reset abuse for account takeover [S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: 300+ active, ~3,800 parked FIFA-lookalike domains; shared Meta Pixel IDs; paid Facebook ads, plus Telegram and WhatsApp links [S3][S4][S7].
diamond.victim: World Cup ticket-buying fans globally; FIFA account holders; 2,500+ FIFA credential pairs reported on dark-web markets (largely infostealer-sourced per one outlet) [S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Opportunistic crime exploiting demand for a mega-event; no political motive indicated in cited sources [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Web phishing, SSO impersonation, social-media advertising, domain parking and rotation [S1][S3].

gaps: Could not open the primary Group-IB report (group-ib.com) or The Record, Infosecurity, BankInfoSecurity pages; all facts rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Hosting providers, registrars, payment channels and IOC lists are not confirmed in reviewed material.
Confidence level and the full technical basis for the Chinese-speaking attribution are not verified.
Relationship between GHOST STADIUM and the other three Group-IB actors, and the Silent Push 227-domain cluster, is unverified.
Loss estimates conflict between Group-IB ($71M-$474M premium tickets) and GovInfoSecurity ($470M-$1B); methodology unseen.
Source of the 2,513 credentials and whether tied to this kit is unclear.
Exact publication dates for several secondary articles are approximate (month level).
Layui 2.7.6, PingIdentity client_id reuse and the November 2025 first-observed date could not be confirmed in search results and were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the operational environment is the commercial internet and social-media ad ecosystem around FIFA World Cup 2026; relevant to DoD mainly through personnel, families and installations in the host or travel context, not military networks. Step 3: the actor is a criminal cluster with scalable kit and domain infrastructure and no stated state ties [S1][S2][S4]. Step 4: MLCOA is continued ad-driven ticket fraud and credential theft with new domains activated through the tournament [S3][S6]; MDCOA is account-takeover reuse of stolen credentials against users who share passwords with official or work accounts (inference). Candidate indicators: hyphenated FIFA-name domains, shared Meta Pixel IDs, SSO-flow clones of fifa.com [S1][S3][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: treat as a force-protection and personnel-awareness issue rather than a threat to mission systems, since the evidence shows consumer-targeted fraud [S1][S4]. Authorities: DoD has no authority to act on commercial fraud infrastructure; takedowns and ad removal go through registrars, Meta and law enforcement. Mission assurance: reduce credential reuse between personal and official accounts and block known lookalike domains on government-managed devices. Coordination: share indicators with Group-IB, Silent Push and relevant law-enforcement/CTI channels through established unclassified sharing paths.
